terms.definition: A dataset where one outcome vastly outnumbers the others, letting a model score well while learning nothing useful.
terms.why_it_matters: It is how "99% accurate" can mean "always predicts no". Ask which metric they used.

terms.definition: Building the pipelines that collect, clean, validate and serve data, along with the storage, schemas and access rules around them.
terms.why_it_matters: This phase decides whether the model is trained on something trustworthy or on quietly rotting inputs.

terms.definition: Pulling data out of source systems into your own storage, in batches or as a stream.
terms.why_it_matters: Ingestion is the boundary you do not control, which is exactly why it needs validation.

terms.definition: Information that would not exist at prediction time leaking into training features, producing offline scores that cannot survive contact with production.
terms.why_it_matters: The classic reason a model that evaluated brilliantly collapses on its first live day.

terms.definition: The recorded path of data from its origin, through every transformation, to the model that consumed it.
terms.why_it_matters: Lineage is how you find every model affected when one upstream source turns out to have been wrong.

terms.definition: The automated flow that moves and transforms data between systems on a schedule or in response to events.
terms.why_it_matters: When a data pipeline breaks overnight, the model keeps serving predictions from whatever it last saw.

terms.definition: How fit data is for its purpose, judged on completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness and validity.
terms.why_it_matters: Nearly every production model failure, traced back far enough, turns out to be a data quality failure.

terms.definition: Automated checks that incoming data matches the expected schema, ranges and distributions before it reaches training or serving.
terms.why_it_matters: The cheapest way to catch a broken upstream feed before it poisons a model in silence.

terms.definition: Keeping immutable, addressable versions of datasets so every model can be tied to exactly the data it learned from.
terms.why_it_matters: Dave's fixed snapshots are data versioning. It is what lets you answer "what changed?" when accuracy drops.

terms.definition: A defined collection of records assembled for a specific purpose, such as training, validating or testing a model.
terms.why_it_matters: "The dataset" is rarely one thing. Ask which version, cut on which date, filtered how.

terms.definition: Extract, Transform, Load: the batch process that moves data out of source systems, reshapes it, and lands it where it can be used.
terms.why_it_matters: Unglamorous plumbing that quietly decides whether the model team has anything to work with.

terms.definition: A single input variable a model reads, derived from raw data, such as "orders in the last seven days".
terms.why_it_matters: Features are where data engineering and model engineering meet, and where they blame each other.

terms.definition: The statistical shape of a feature's values: its range, spread and frequencies.
terms.why_it_matters: A model learns a distribution, not a world. When the distribution moves, the learning quietly expires.

terms.definition: Designing and computing the input variables a model learns from, turning raw records into signals with predictive value.
terms.why_it_matters: Often the highest-leverage work on a model, and the hardest to hand to someone else.

terms.definition: A shared service that computes, stores and serves features so that training and serving use the same definitions and the same values.
terms.why_it_matters: The standard cure for training-serving skew, priced at one more platform component to operate.

terms.definition: The known correct answer attached to a training example, and the thing a supervised model learns to predict.
terms.why_it_matters: Labels are expensive, usually delayed, and in production often arrive far too late to catch a problem early.

terms.definition: The formal contract describing a dataset's fields, their types and their allowed values.
terms.why_it_matters: A schema is what turns a silent upstream change into a loud, catchable error.

terms.definition: An upstream source quietly changing its fields, types, units or encoding.
terms.why_it_matters: This is Dave's warning in the data phase: nothing errors, the numbers simply start meaning something else.

terms.definition: A frozen copy of a data source at one moment, used so a training run has a stable, reproducible input.
terms.why_it_matters: Snapshots buy stability and pay for it in staleness. That trade is the whole Data Instability challenge.

terms.definition: Data that no longer reflects the current world because the snapshot behind it has not been refreshed.
terms.why_it_matters: Ruth's objection in one line: a frozen snapshot stops surprising you, and also stops being true.

terms.definition: The examples a model learns from.
terms.why_it_matters: Everything the model believes about the world, it believes because this set told it so.

terms.definition: Sprawling, unreviewed configuration where a single wrong value quietly changes model behaviour with no test to catch it.
terms.why_it_matters: Configuration is code that nobody reviews, and it ships to production more often than code does.

terms.definition: A model's reliance on an input owned by someone else, who may change or retire it on their own schedule.
terms.why_it_matters: Data dependencies cost more than code dependencies and almost nobody tracks them with the same care.

terms.definition: In an ML model, changing anything changes everything: alter one feature's weight, distribution or presence and every other feature's contribution shifts too.
terms.why_it_matters: The Entanglement Problem challenge. It is why you cannot improve one part of a model in isolation and prove it.

terms.definition: A model influencing the world that generates its next training data, so it ends up learning from its own past behaviour.
terms.why_it_matters: Loops make offline evaluation optimistic and make cause and effect very hard to separate afterwards.

terms.definition: The mass of adapter code written to connect general-purpose ML packages to a specific system, which ends up outweighing the modelling code.
terms.why_it_matters: It is where most of the maintenance goes, and nobody puts it on a roadmap.

terms.definition: The argument that ML systems accumulate maintenance cost in ways ordinary software does not, because data dependencies and feedback loops erode a system even while its code sits still.
terms.why_it_matters: Two of this game's challenges come straight from that paper. The debt is invisible until you try to change something.

terms.definition: Data preparation grown by accretion into a thicket of scrapes, joins and one-off steps that only works because nobody has touched it.
terms.why_it_matters: The predictable end state of always adding one more signal under time pressure.

terms.definition: The future cost of a shortcut taken today: the extra work every later change has to pay because the quick solution was kept.
terms.why_it_matters: ML systems accrue it faster than ordinary software, because data and models rot even when the code never changes.

terms.definition: Features being computed one way during training and a subtly different way at serving time, so the live model sees inputs it was never trained on.
terms.why_it_matters: A silent accuracy killer that no offline evaluation can reveal, and the main argument for a feature store.

terms.definition: A downstream team quietly depending on your model's output without telling you, so your next change breaks something you did not know existed.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the reason a harmless-looking model update takes down an unrelated dashboard.

terms.definition: Checks a pipeline runs on its own before promoting a model: performance thresholds, data checks, fairness tests, smoke tests.
terms.why_it_matters: The Automation Risk challenge in one phrase. It catches what you thought to encode, and nothing else.

terms.definition: Scoring a large set of records on a schedule and storing the results for later lookup.
terms.why_it_matters: Far cheaper and calmer than real-time serving, and impossible when the answer must reflect the last few seconds.

terms.definition: Keeping two complete environments and switching traffic from the old to the new in one move, with the old kept warm for instant reversal.
terms.why_it_matters: Buys a fast, boring rollback at the price of running two of everything.

terms.definition: Releasing a change to a small slice of traffic first and widening only while the metrics hold.
terms.why_it_matters: The compromise between Alex's full automation and Reuben's demand that a human check the result.

terms.definition: Running a trained model on new input to produce an output.
terms.why_it_matters: Inference is what the user actually experiences, and it is where latency and cost per call are measured.

terms.definition: Moving a trained model into a production system where real users or services consume its predictions.
terms.why_it_matters: The moment a model stops being an experiment and starts producing real business and compliance risk.

terms.definition: The infrastructure that hosts a model behind an interface and answers prediction requests reliably and at scale.
terms.why_it_matters: Serving is a production service with uptime obligations, not an attachment to a model.

terms.definition: Scoring a single request on demand, inside a live user interaction, under a latency budget.
terms.why_it_matters: This is the mode where Emilia's 50ms ceiling turns into an architecture constraint.

terms.definition: The live environment serving real traffic, where failure has real consequences, as opposed to a notebook or sandbox.
terms.why_it_matters: Whoever owns production values stability far above the last percent of accuracy, and they are not being difficult.

terms.definition: Returning to the previously known-good version after a release misbehaves.
terms.why_it_matters: A deployment plan without a rehearsed rollback is a plan to argue during an incident.

terms.definition: Running a new model alongside the live one on real traffic while discarding its output, purely to compare behaviour.
terms.why_it_matters: Lets you earn confidence on production data without exposing a single user to the new model.

terms.definition: An automated check that one piece of a system behaves as specified, run on every change.
terms.why_it_matters: ML code is testable like any other code; the models are the part that need a different kind of gate.

terms.definition: Keeping enough record of data, code, approvals and decisions that an outsider can reconstruct what happened and when.
terms.why_it_matters: Auditability is why an approval step that feels like bureaucracy is sometimes genuinely non-negotiable.

terms.definition: A systematic skew in data or model behaviour that disadvantages particular groups or outcomes.
terms.why_it_matters: Bias is inherited from data by default. Not looking for it is a decision, not a neutral position.

terms.definition: Meeting the legal and policy obligations that apply to the system, and being able to demonstrate that you do.
terms.why_it_matters: Compliance requirements do not negotiate, and the stakeholder repeating them is usually the one who will be held responsible.

terms.definition: Being able to say why a model produced a particular output, in terms a human, an auditor or an affected person can follow.
terms.why_it_matters: Often a hard constraint in regulated settings, and one that quietly rules out the most complex architectures.

terms.definition: Whether a model's errors and benefits fall evenly across groups of people, rather than concentrating on some of them.
terms.why_it_matters: Aggregate accuracy hides this completely, which is why a fairness check is a separate gate.

terms.definition: Keeping a person in a decision path, either reviewing outputs or approving a promotion, instead of letting the system act alone.
terms.why_it_matters: Reuben's position: some judgements, especially fairness ones, cannot be delegated to a test suite.

terms.definition: A short standard document recording a model's intended use, training data, evaluation results and known limitations.
terms.why_it_matters: The cheapest artefact that stops a model being used for something it was never validated for.

terms.definition: The controls around models in production: who may approve, promote, change or retire one, and on what evidence.
terms.why_it_matters: Governance is the machinery that makes an agreement survive the departure of the people who made it.

terms.definition: Building and running ML systems so their effects on people are examined and defensible: fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy and safety.
terms.why_it_matters: Reuben's objection to full automation lives here, and it is the one that carries regulatory teeth.

terms.definition: Protecting data, models and infrastructure from unauthorised access, alteration or exfiltration.
terms.why_it_matters: Security requirements shape where data may live, which reshapes the whole architecture underneath.

terms.definition: Grouping several requests so they are processed together, raising throughput per unit of hardware.
terms.why_it_matters: Improves cost per prediction and adds waiting time, which is exactly the wrong direction under a latency cap.

terms.definition: Choosing between building tooling that fits your requirements exactly and adopting a vendor product that fits most of them today.
terms.why_it_matters: Buying converts engineering effort into a subscription and a dependency. Building converts it into a permanent maintenance obligation.

terms.definition: Keeping recent or precomputed results close to where they are needed so repeat work is skipped.
terms.why_it_matters: A common way to buy back latency without simplifying the model, as long as the cached answer is still valid.

terms.definition: What running the workload actually costs, including training compute, serving capacity, storage and data movement.
terms.why_it_matters: Model complexity is usually paid monthly. That is why the efficiency stakeholder keeps reappearing.

terms.definition: Packaging code with its dependencies into a portable image that runs identically wherever it is deployed.
terms.why_it_matters: The usual fix for "it worked in training" being different from "it works in serving".

terms.definition: Specialised hardware that makes training and heavy inference far faster, at a substantial hourly price.
terms.why_it_matters: The most visible line item when someone asks why the model budget doubled.

terms.definition: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled files so environments can be recreated and reviewed like software.
terms.why_it_matters: It is what makes an environment reproducible, which is a precondition for a reproducible model.

terms.definition: An orchestration system that schedules, scales and restarts containerised workloads across a cluster.
terms.why_it_matters: Powerful, and an operational commitment of its own. Someone has to run the thing that runs your model.

terms.definition: The integrated tooling a team uses to run the ML lifecycle: pipelines, tracking, registry, serving and monitoring in one place.
terms.why_it_matters: The Platform Choice challenge is a build-versus-buy decision about exactly this.

terms.definition: Software run and operated by a vendor and consumed over the network for a recurring fee.
terms.why_it_matters: Predictable monthly pricing is Emilia's stated constraint, and it is a real one for anyone defending a budget.

terms.definition: A system's ability to handle more load by adding resources, without a redesign.
terms.why_it_matters: "It works on my laptop" and "it works at peak traffic" are different claims with different price tags.

terms.definition: Depending on one supplier's proprietary interfaces so heavily that leaving would mean rebuilding.
terms.why_it_matters: The cost that never appears in the first year's pricing comparison.

terms.definition: Any versioned output of the pipeline that later steps depend on: a dataset, a trained model, an evaluation report.
terms.why_it_matters: Treating outputs as named artifacts, not files on someone's machine, is what makes a pipeline auditable.

terms.definition: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery: automatically building, testing and releasing changes so small updates ship often and safely.
terms.why_it_matters: Alex pushes CI/CD because manual releases are slow and error-prone. The counter-argument is that automation also removes the human who would have said no.

terms.definition: Extending CI/CD to the model itself: the pipeline retrains and re-evaluates automatically when fresh data or a drift alarm arrives.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the standard answer to drift, and the standard fear is that it silently promotes a worse model.

terms.definition: Recording every training run together with its code version, data version, hyperparameters and metrics, so runs can be compared and rebuilt.
terms.why_it_matters: It turns "the model that worked last Tuesday" into something you can actually retrieve.

terms.definition: The point where work passes from one team to another, for instance data science handing a trained model to operations.
terms.why_it_matters: Most friction in this game lives at hand-offs, where one group's finished work becomes another group's problem.

terms.definition: The end-to-end loop a model travels: requirements, data engineering, model engineering, deployment, monitoring, and back around to retraining.
terms.why_it_matters: The phases you play follow this loop. A decision taken early keeps charging you rent in every later phase.

terms.definition: Development that repeats the same sequence of phases, each pass starting from what the last one built rather than from scratch.
terms.why_it_matters: Reaching monitoring is not the end of the work. The next pass reopens requirements with production evidence in hand - and with every component you already raised still standing.

terms.definition: An automated chain of steps (ingest, validate, transform, train, evaluate, register, deploy) that turns raw data into a deployable model with no manual hand-offs in the middle.
terms.why_it_matters: A pipeline is what makes a result reproducible. A notebook run by one person cannot be rerun the same way six months later.

terms.definition: The practice of running machine learning in production: joining ML, software engineering and operations so models are built, shipped, monitored and retrained on a repeatable pipeline instead of by hand.
terms.why_it_matters: Every phase of this game is one stage of the MLOps lifecycle. The stakeholders argue because each of them owns a different stage.

terms.definition: A ladder describing how automated an organisation's ML practice is, from manual notebooks, through automated training pipelines, to full CI/CD/CT.
terms.why_it_matters: Useful shorthand when stakeholders argue about how much process is enough for the team they actually have.

terms.definition: A catalogue of trained models with their versions, lineage, evaluation results and promotion status (staging, production, archived).
terms.why_it_matters: It is the single place that answers "what exactly is serving right now, and who approved it?"

terms.definition: Giving every trained model an immutable identity tied to its code, data and configuration.
terms.why_it_matters: Rollback, audit and blame all depend on being able to name the exact version that misbehaved.

terms.definition: An interactive document mixing code, output and notes, and the usual place ML work starts.
terms.why_it_matters: Excellent for exploring, poor at reproducing. Most MLOps effort is spent getting work out of one.

terms.definition: The ability to rerun a training job later with the same code, data and configuration and get the same model back.
terms.why_it_matters: Without it you cannot debug a regression, defend a result to an auditor, or roll back with any confidence.

terms.definition: Splitting live traffic between two versions and comparing an agreed metric to decide which actually performs better.
terms.why_it_matters: The only measurement that settles "better for the business" rather than "better on the test set".

terms.definition: The share of predictions that are correct.
terms.why_it_matters: The most quoted and least informative metric. On imbalanced data a high figure can mean the model never says yes.

terms.definition: How well a model ranks positives above negatives across every possible threshold.
terms.why_it_matters: Threshold-free, which makes it good for comparing models and poor for describing live behaviour.

terms.definition: The outcome the organisation actually cares about, such as revenue, retention, cost saved or time saved.
terms.why_it_matters: Emilia's recurring point: model metrics only count once someone shows they move a business metric.

terms.definition: The table of predicted against actual outcomes, splitting errors into false positives and false negatives.
terms.why_it_matters: It shows which kind of mistake the model makes, which is the part the business actually feels.

terms.definition: Rotating which slice of the data is held out, training several times, and averaging the scores for a more stable estimate.
terms.why_it_matters: Buys a more honest performance number for more compute, which is a trade Emilia will notice.

terms.definition: The score above which a model's output is treated as a positive decision.
terms.why_it_matters: Moving the threshold changes precision and recall with no retraining, and is often the fastest lever available.

terms.definition: Measuring a model against agreed metrics on data it did not learn from, before anyone decides to ship it.
terms.why_it_matters: Whoever defines the evaluation set has quietly defined what "good" means for the whole project.

terms.definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving one number when both matter and neither may collapse.
terms.why_it_matters: Useful when someone demands a single figure and accuracy would flatter the model.

terms.definition: How well a model performs on data it has never seen, as opposed to data it was fitted to.
terms.why_it_matters: The only performance that survives deployment. Everything else is a rehearsal.

terms.definition: Of everything the model flagged, the share that really was positive.
terms.why_it_matters: This is the metric you care about when a false alarm is expensive.

terms.definition: Of everything that really was positive, the share the model actually caught.
terms.why_it_matters: This is the metric you care about when a miss is expensive. It usually trades against precision.

terms.definition: Data held back from training and used once, at the end, to estimate performance on inputs the model has never seen.
terms.why_it_matters: Monica's 95% target is measured here, so how the split was made matters as much as the number.

terms.definition: A second held-back split used during development to tune choices, keeping the test set clean for the final estimate.
terms.why_it_matters: Reusing the test set to tune is how teams talk themselves into a number they cannot reproduce.

terms.definition: The simplest reasonable model or rule used as a reference point, so any complex alternative has to prove it earns its complexity.
terms.why_it_matters: The most useful question in a model debate: how much better is this than the boring option?

terms.definition: Models built from many layers of learned transformations, powerful on unstructured data and expensive in data, compute and interpretability.
terms.why_it_matters: Monica's preferred hammer. Its costs land on Emilia's budget and Ruth's pager.

terms.definition: Combining several component models and merging their outputs, so no single model has to carry every signal.
terms.why_it_matters: Dave's answer to entanglement: isolate the signals so one change stops moving everything at once.

terms.definition: A setting chosen before training rather than learned from data, such as learning rate, depth or regularisation strength.
terms.why_it_matters: Tuning them is where a lot of compute budget silently disappears.

terms.definition: The structural choice behind a model: its type, its layers or components, and how information flows through it.
terms.why_it_matters: Architecture sets the floor on inference cost and latency long before anyone tunes anything.

terms.definition: How much capacity and structure a model carries, in parameters, components and interactions.
terms.why_it_matters: Complexity is paid for in compute, latency, debugging time and every future change. It rarely appears on the accuracy slide.

terms.definition: Designing, training, tuning and evaluating candidate models until one is good enough to promote toward production.
terms.why_it_matters: Where accuracy ambitions collide with the cost and latency limits agreed in earlier phases.

terms.definition: A model learning the noise and quirks of its training data instead of the pattern, so it scores well there and poorly everywhere else.
terms.why_it_matters: A suspiciously high training score is a warning, not an achievement.

terms.definition: Deliberately constraining a model during training to discourage it from fitting noise.
terms.why_it_matters: A cheap lever for generalisation that costs a little training-set accuracy, which some stakeholders will read as a loss.

terms.definition: Fitting a model's parameters to data by repeatedly measuring error and adjusting.
terms.why_it_matters: Training cost is recurring, not one-off, once you commit to retraining on a schedule.

terms.definition: A model too simple to capture the real pattern, performing poorly on training and new data alike.
terms.why_it_matters: The honest failure mode. At least it is visible before deployment.

terms.definition: Automatic notification when a monitored signal crosses a threshold that a human needs to know about.
terms.why_it_matters: Alerts nobody trusts are worse than no alerts, because they train the team to look away.

terms.definition: The relationship between inputs and the correct answer itself changing, so the old pattern is now wrong even on familiar-looking data.
terms.why_it_matters: Worse than data drift: retraining on recent data helps only once you can tell which kind you have.

terms.definition: The live input distribution moving away from the one the model was trained on, so its learned assumptions stop matching reality.
terms.why_it_matters: The declining accuracy in the final phase is drift. Nothing in the code changed; the world did.

terms.definition: An unplanned disruption to a live service, and by extension the process of responding to and learning from one.
terms.why_it_matters: The people who carry the pager weigh every proposal by how it will read at 3am.

terms.definition: How long a single request takes to answer, usually quoted at a high percentile rather than as an average.
terms.why_it_matters: Emilia's 50ms ceiling is a latency budget, and every layer of model complexity spends part of it.

terms.definition: A deployed model's real-world performance eroding over time as data and behaviour move on.
terms.why_it_matters: Decay is the default state of a deployed model. Retraining is maintenance, not a bug fix.

terms.definition: Continuously watching a live system's inputs, outputs, performance and health, and raising an alert when they leave the expected range.
terms.why_it_matters: Models fail silently. Without monitoring the first person to notice is a customer, or a regulator.

terms.definition: Being able to work out what a system is doing internally from the signals it emits, rather than only whether it is up.
terms.why_it_matters: Monitoring tells you something broke. Observability is what lets you find out why before the meeting.

terms.definition: How consistently a system does the right thing under real conditions, including load, partial failures and bad input.
terms.why_it_matters: Ruth's whole agenda. It is measured over months, which is why it always loses a demo and wins a review.

terms.definition: Fitting a new version of a model on fresher data, then evaluating it against the incumbent before it replaces anything.
terms.why_it_matters: Ruth's warning: retraining without diagnosis locks in whatever went wrong, and does it faster next time.

terms.definition: Working back from a symptom to the underlying cause, instead of treating whichever surface fault is easiest to reach.
terms.why_it_matters: "Accuracy dropped, retrain it" skips this step, which is exactly the objection raised against a rapid fix.

terms.definition: A committed level of service (uptime, latency, freshness), usually with agreed consequences when it is missed.
terms.why_it_matters: An SLA turns a preference about speed into a contractual hard constraint. Check which one you are being handed.

terms.definition: How many requests a system can serve per unit of time.
terms.why_it_matters: Latency and throughput are traded against each other by batching, which helps one and hurts the other.

terms.definition: The concrete, checkable conditions a deliverable must meet before stakeholders consider it finished.
terms.why_it_matters: "Accurate enough" is not acceptance criteria. "95% on the agreed test set" is.

terms.definition: Actively drawing requirements out of stakeholders through interviews, documents, observation and workshops, rather than waiting for them to be written down.
terms.why_it_matters: The intel phases are elicitation. What people volunteer is never the whole constraint set.

terms.definition: A statement of what the system must do: an input, a behaviour, an output.
terms.why_it_matters: Easy to agree on and rarely the thing that sinks an ML project.

terms.definition: A requirement that cannot be traded away: violating it makes the solution unacceptable, regardless of what it gains elsewhere.
terms.why_it_matters: Mistagging a hard constraint as a preference is the most expensive filing error you can make in this game.

terms.definition: Something a stakeholder would like, stated as a want rather than a limit, and tradeable against other goals.
terms.why_it_matters: Preferences are your negotiating currency. Spend them to protect the constraints that really are hard.

terms.definition: A requirement about how well the system must behave rather than what it does: latency, cost, availability, security, maintainability.
terms.why_it_matters: Latency ceilings, budget caps and audit rules are all NFRs, and they are what usually kills an otherwise accurate model.

terms.definition: A grid sorting stakeholders by how much influence they hold and how much they care, used to decide who to manage closely and who to merely keep informed.
terms.why_it_matters: High power, low interest is the dangerous quadrant: they are not paying attention until they veto you.

terms.definition: Eliciting, negotiating and recording what a system must do, and getting the people who care about it to agree on that record before it is built.
terms.why_it_matters: This is your actual job here: turn what stakeholders say into requirements all of them will sign.

terms.definition: Requirements quietly expanding after the plan was agreed, without a matching adjustment to time, budget or staffing.
terms.why_it_matters: Most scope creep enters as a reasonable-sounding preference from someone senior.

terms.definition: Anyone whose interests are affected by the system: users, owners, operators, regulators, and the teams who must maintain it.
terms.why_it_matters: The ones who can block you are rarely the ones who asked for the project.

terms.definition: The state where the people who can approve, fund or block a system agree on what it is for and what it must not do.
terms.why_it_matters: Alignment, not accuracy, is what gets a model into production in a real organisation.

terms.definition: Keeping a link from each requirement to its source stakeholder and to the design and test that satisfy it.
terms.why_it_matters: When a constraint is challenged later, traceability is how you prove where it came from.
